4480:
Discredit means the loss of trust, respect, or good reputation — either the process of losing it, or the damaged state that results.

Think of it this way: every person, organization, or institution holds a kind of "credit" with others — a store of trust, belief, and respect. When that store is damaged or destroyed, you have discredit. It's what's left when a good name is ruined.

The noun "discredit" carries two shades of meaning that overlap heavily:

Sense 1: The state or condition of having lost respect or trust.

This is when someone or something is no longer believed, valued, or respected by others. They have fallen into discredit — meaning people now view them with suspicion, doubt, or contempt.

After the forgery was exposed, the historian fell into complete discredit.

Here, "discredit" names the condition the historian now exists in — a state where no one trusts his work anymore.

Sense 2: Something that causes harm to a reputation — a source of shame or disgrace.

Here, "discredit" refers to the person, action, or fact that brings the damage. It is used to say that someone or something is a stain on a group, a profession, or a cause.

His greed was a discredit to the entire charity.
Such behavior brings discredit upon the whole institution.

Here, "discredit" names the damage caused — the thing dragging the reputation down.

In Sense 1, discredit is the wound itself — the damaged reputation.
In Sense 2, discredit is the cause of the wound — something that inflicts the damage.

But in practice, both senses revolve around the same central idea: a reputation being harmed in the eyes of others. Context makes it clear which sense is meant.
What Discredit Looks Like in Real Life

Discredit is not a private feeling — it is always social. It happens in the eyes of an audience. If nobody sees, nobody judges, and no reputation changes, there is no discredit.

A few situations where discredit occurs:

  • A scientist whose research is proven to be fabricated falls into discredit — the scientific community no longer treats their work as credible.
  • A soldier who deserts their post is called a discredit to their regiment — their actions damage the good name of the whole unit.
  • A company caught lying to customers brings discredit upon its entire industry — it makes the whole field look dishonest.

Notice that discredit always involves others changing how they see you (or a group you belong to). It is about standing in the world, not just internal guilt.

Discredit always flows from an act or fact to a person, group, or idea:

  • An act of cowardice → brings discredit → upon a soldier
  • A proven lie → brings discredit → upon a leader
  • A corrupt member → reflects discredit → upon the whole organization

This is why you will often see it used with words like "bring," "cast," "fall into," "reflect," and "to someone's discredit."

This is one of the most common ways the noun is used. It means: this fact harms that person's reputation; it counts against them.

To his discredit, he never apologized for what he did.

This construction is often used when the speaker is making a fair judgment — acknowledging something that reflects poorly on a person, even if other things reflect well.

Its opposite is "to someone's credit" — meaning something that makes them look good.

Discredit exists on a spectrum:

  • Mild discredit: A small blemish on someone's reputation. People are slightly less impressed or trusting.
  • Moderate discredit: A real dent — people become noticeably skeptical or dismissive.
  • Complete/total discredit: The reputation is entirely destroyed. Nobody believes, respects, or takes the person seriously anymore.

Common intensifiers you'll see with it: total discredit, complete discredit, utter discredit, great discredit.

Understanding where "discredit" sits among similar words helps sharpen its meaning:

  • Disgrace — stronger and more emotional; implies moral shame, often including public humiliation. Disgrace is about shame; discredit is about lost trust and damaged standing.
  • Dishonor — relates to a violation of a code (of honor, duty, or dignity). More formal and often used in contexts of military, family, or moral duty.
  • Disrepute — very close to discredit; both refer to a bad reputation in the eyes of others. Disrepute tends to describe a general low standing ("fallen into disrepute"), while discredit more often emphasizes the act of damaging or the resulting loss of credibility specifically.
  • Shame — an internal feeling; discredit is external (what others think of you). You can feel shame privately; discredit requires an audience.

Discredit (noun) = the loss or damage of a good reputation, credibility, or trust in the eyes of others — either the damaged state someone is in, or the act/thing that causes that damage.

It is always social, always visible to others, and always involves a fall from good standing to doubt, distrust, or contempt.
4481:
At the heart of this word is credit — and here, "credit" doesn't mean money. It means trust, belief, and good reputation. When you give someone credit, you believe them and respect them. When you *dis*credit someone, you do the opposite — you take that trust away.

So, to discredit means to cause people to stop believing in, trusting, or respecting someone or something.

This verb works in two slightly different but deeply connected ways.

1. To damage a person's reputation or credibility

This is when someone causes others to view a person as untrustworthy, unreliable, or dishonest — so that people no longer take that person seriously.

"The politician tried to discredit his opponent by digging up old scandals."

Here, the goal is to make people think: "Why should I believe or trust this person?" The target's credibility — their standing as a believable, reliable person — gets damaged or destroyed.

2. To cause an idea, theory, claim, or piece of evidence to seem false or unreliable

This is when something — not a person, but a statement, belief, or argument — is shown to be unworthy of belief.

"The new experiment discredited the old theory completely."
"Her testimony was discredited when the security footage told a different story."

Here, the idea or claim loses its trustworthiness. People stop accepting it as true or valid.

Both meanings share one common thread: something or someone loses their credibility — their power to be believed or trusted. Whether it's a person's reputation or an argument's validity, the result is the same: people say "I can no longer trust this."
Can It Be Done Fairly or Unfairly?

Yes — and this is an important nuance. Discrediting can be:

Fair and legitimate — when it's done using real evidence and honest reasoning. A scientist discredits a flawed study with better data. A lawyer discredits a lying witness with proof of their lies. In these cases, discrediting is a healthy, necessary thing.

Unfair and malicious — when it's done with the intention of destroying someone's reputation, often using twisted information, half-truths, or attacks on character rather than substance. Politicians do this to rivals. Corporations do this to whistleblowers. In these cases, discrediting is manipulative and harmful.

The word itself is neutral — it doesn't tell you whether the discrediting is justified or not. Context does that job.

Discrediting is not a mild thing. It's not the same as simply doubting someone. To discredit something is to significantly undermine or destroy its credibility — not just raise a small question, but cause a serious, lasting collapse of trust. If a theory is discredited, scientists largely abandon it. If a witness is discredited, their entire account is treated as unreliable.
Who or What Can Be Discredited

Almost anything that relies on being believed or trusted can be discredited:

A person — a politician, a scientist, a witness, an expert, a journalist, a leader.

An idea or theory — a scientific hypothesis, a political argument, a conspiracy theory.

A claim or statement — an accusation, an alibi, a rumor, an announcement.

Evidence — a document, a piece of testimony, a statistic, a report.

An institution — a court, a news organization, a government body.
How It Behaves in a Sentence

Discredit always needs an object — something or someone being discredited. You don't just "discredit"; you discredit someone or something.

It is often used with words like "try to," "attempt to," "seek to," or "manage to" — because discrediting is usually a deliberate act that takes effort:

"They tried to discredit the investigation."
"She managed to discredit the key witness."
"His own actions discredited him."

It also appears very naturally in the passive voice — meaning the subject is the one receiving the damage:

"The theory has been completely discredited."
"He was discredited by his own allies."
How It Differs from Similar Words

Disprove means to show with solid evidence that something is factually false. Discrediting doesn't always go that far — it makes something seem untrustworthy without necessarily proving it false. You can discredit a person by questioning their character, not just their facts.

Defame or slander means attacking someone's reputation — usually with lies. Discrediting is broader; it can involve true information used to destroy trust, or simply casting doubt without outright lying.

Undermine means to weaken something gradually from beneath — it can apply to confidence, authority, plans, or morale. Discredit is more specific: it always targets credibility and trustworthiness in particular.

Debunk means to expose a belief, myth, or claim as false or exaggerated. It's close to discrediting an idea, but debunking always implies that the thing was false all along. Discrediting focuses more on the process of destroying trust, and it applies to people too.

To credit, validate, vindicate, or endorse someone is the opposite — it means to vouch for their trustworthiness, confirm that their claims are reliable, or restore their reputation. If someone was wrongly discredited, they might later be vindicated — meaning their credibility is restored and their name is cleared.
A Final Way to Remember It

Think of credibility as a currency of trust. Everyone — every person, every idea, every argument — has some amount of this currency stored up. To discredit is to drain that currency until people no longer accept it as valid. Once someone is discredited, their words bounce like a bad check — nobody accepts them anymore.
4482:
"Discreet" describes a person or action that is carefully tactful and private — especially when handling sensitive, delicate, or confidential matters. A discreet person knows what to say, what not to say, when to speak, and when to stay completely silent, all to avoid causing trouble, embarrassment, or unwanted attention.

Think of it this way: if someone shares a personal secret with you and you never mention it to anyone, never bring it up at the wrong moment, and never let on that you even know it — you are being discreet.
The Heart of the Word: Good Judgment in Sensitive Situations

"Discreet" is not simply about being quiet. It is about exercising careful judgment when you are dealing with something sensitive. A truly discreet person is always thinking: Should I say this? To whom? When? How?

A lawyer who knows damaging information about a client but handles it with great care and never reveals it unnecessarily is being discreet. A friend who witnesses an awkward moment between a couple and pretends not to notice is being discreet. The common thread is always the same: thoughtful restraint in the face of something delicate.
The Two Main Ways "Discreet" Is Used

The first and most common use is about keeping things private. When someone is discreet, they handle confidential or sensitive information carefully and do not reveal it to people who have no business knowing it.

For example: "She was very discreet about her colleague's health problems — she never breathed a word to anyone." Or: "The police conducted a discreet investigation — almost no one in town knew it was happening."

The second use is about being subtle and unobtrusive — not flashy, not loud, not drawing unnecessary attention. Something "discreet" in this sense is understated and quiet by design.

For example: "He wore a discreet pin on his jacket — small, simple, and barely noticeable." Or: "The bodyguard stood at a discreet distance — close enough to help, but far enough not to crowd anyone." Or: "They chose a discreet location for the meeting — a quiet café away from the busy streets."

In practice, both meanings often blend together. When someone says "please be discreet about this," they usually mean: don't talk about it AND don't be obvious about the fact that you know something. Tactful silence plus understated behavior, together.
What "Discreet" Looks Like in Everyday Sentences

To truly absorb a word, you need to see it doing real work. Here are varied examples that cover the full range:

"The doctor was always discreet about her patients — she never discussed their cases in public."
(= careful and private)

"He gave her a discreet nod from across the room."
(= a small, subtle gesture that only she could notice)

"I need someone discreet for this job — someone who can ask questions without raising suspicions."
(= someone who is careful and does not draw attention)

"The company offers discreet packaging for all orders."
(= packaging that gives nothing away about what is inside — very common in online shopping)

"She discreetly slipped out of the party early without making a scene."
(Here "discreetly" is the adverb form — she left quietly and without fuss)

"He could have announced her mistake in front of everyone, but instead he pulled her aside and gave her a discreet warning."
(= a quiet, private warning rather than a public embarrassment)
Discreet vs. Discrete — A Crucial Distinction

These two words are so similar in spelling that even native speakers confuse them. As a learner, it is essential that you know the difference.

Discreet (with the two e's close together) means careful, tactful, and private — everything we have discussed here.

Discrete (with the two e's separated by a "t") is a completely unrelated word meaning separate, distinct, or individually separate. For example: "The course is divided into five discrete modules" means five separate, distinct modules.

A helpful trick: discreet is connected to the noun discretion. If you can replace the word with "discretion" or "discreetly," you want the spelling d-i-s-c-r-e-e-t. If the meaning is "separate" or "distinct," you want d-i-s-c-r-e-t-e.
The Word Family You Should Know

Since the goal is to never need another source, here are the related forms of the word:

Discretion (noun) is what a discreet person has. "Handle this with discretion." It also appears in the phrase "at your discretion," meaning "according to your own judgment." "You may leave early at your discretion" = you can decide for yourself.

Discreetly (adverb) means in a discreet manner. "She discreetly passed him the note."

Indiscreet (adjective) is the opposite — someone who is tactless, who reveals things carelessly, who blurts out secrets or says the wrong thing at the wrong time. "It was indiscreet of him to mention her salary in front of everyone."

Indiscretion (noun) is an indiscreet act or remark — a moment where someone said or did something they should not have. "His youthful indiscretions came back to haunt him."
What a Discreet Person Is NOT

A discreet person is not a gossip. They are not someone who reveals secrets, draws unnecessary attention to sensitive matters, blurts things out impulsively, or makes a scene when quiet restraint is called for. If someone is described as "not very discreet," it means they talk too freely, reveal things carelessly, or behave in ways that embarrass or expose others.

Discreet means being carefully tactful and private — knowing what to say and what not to say, when to act and when to hold back, especially in sensitive or confidential situations — all without drawing unwanted attention.
4483:
A discrepancy is a difference between two or more things that should match or agree with each other — but don't.

The key part of that definition is "should match." A discrepancy isn't just any difference. It's a difference that feels wrong, unexpected, or problematic — because logic, rules, facts, or expectation say the two things ought to be the same.

Think of it as a mismatch that raises a flag.
A Simple, Everyday Example

Imagine you work at a shop. At the end of the day, the cash register says you collected $500. But when you count the actual cash in the drawer, you only have $470.

Those two numbers should be the same. But they're not. That gap of $30 is a discrepancy.

Nobody just shrugs and walks away from it. It demands an explanation: Was money stolen? Was a sale recorded wrongly? The discrepancy signals that something needs to be investigated.
What Makes "Discrepancy" Different from Just Saying "Difference"

This is important to understand, because students often wonder: Why not just say "difference"?

The word "difference" is neutral. If you say "there's a difference between a cat and a dog," that's just an observation. Nobody is alarmed. No one needs to fix anything.

But the word "discrepancy" carries a built-in sense of concern or conflict. It suggests:

  • The two things should have matched, based on some standard, rule, or expectation.
  • They didn't match.
  • This gap is worth noticing, questioning, or resolving.

So "discrepancy" is a loaded word. It doesn't just describe a difference — it signals a problem with that difference.
The Three Key Elements of Every Discrepancy

Whenever you encounter or use the word "discrepancy," three things are almost always present:

1. Two (or more) things being compared
There's always a comparison happening — two numbers, two accounts, two measurements, two statements, etc.

2. An expectation of agreement
There's a reason those two things should be the same or consistent. A rule, a standard, logic, or common sense sets that expectation.

3. A gap or conflict
The two things don't match up, and that gap is the discrepancy itself.
More Examples Across Different Situations

In finances:
Your bank statement says your account balance is $1,200. But your own spending records show it should be $1,350. The $150 gap is a discrepancy. A bank error or a forgotten transaction could explain it.

In science:
A scientist runs an experiment and expects a result of 98°C based on theory. The actual result is 84°C. That 14-degree discrepancy tells the scientist something is wrong — either with the theory, the equipment, or the method.

In stories and testimonies:
Two witnesses describe the same car accident. One says the red car ran a red light. The other says the light was green. Their accounts don't match. There's a discrepancy in their testimonies. A judge or investigator must figure out who is correct.

In everyday life:
A job posting says the salary is $60,000. But when you get the actual offer letter, it says $52,000. That's a discrepancy — and a very important one you'd want resolved before accepting the job.

In data and records:
A student's school report says she attended 180 days. But the official attendance log only shows 160 days. The 20-day discrepancy needs an explanation.
How Big Does a Discrepancy Have to Be?

A discrepancy can be large or small. What matters is not the size of the gap, but whether the gap matters in context.

A 1-second discrepancy in someone's alibi for a murder investigation could be enormously significant. A 1-second discrepancy in when your coffee finished brewing means nothing to anyone.

So the word itself doesn't tell you how serious the problem is — context decides that. But the word always tells you: these two things don't agree, and they should.
The Tone and Register of the Word

"Discrepancy" is a formal, serious-sounding word. You'll see it most often in:

  • Legal documents and court proceedings
  • Financial reports and audits
  • Scientific research and data analysis
  • Official investigations and reports
  • Journalism and formal writing

In casual speech, people are more likely to say "they don't match," "something doesn't add up," or "there's a gap." But when precision and formality matter — like in a report, an investigation, or a professional document — "discrepancy" is exactly the right word.
The Plural: Discrepancies

The plural form, discrepancies, simply means more than one such mismatch exists.

"The auditors found several discrepancies in the company's financial records."

This means they found multiple places where numbers, facts, or records didn't add up the way they should have.
Common Word Pairings (Collocations)

Certain words naturally appear alongside "discrepancy." Learning these helps you use and recognize the word naturally:

  • Find / found a discrepancy — "Investigators found a discrepancy in the report."
  • Spot / notice a discrepancy — "She noticed a discrepancy between the two documents."
  • Explain a discrepancy — "Can you explain this discrepancy in your accounts?"
  • Resolve a discrepancy — "We need to resolve the discrepancy before filing the report."
  • A significant / major discrepancy — "There's a significant discrepancy in the test results."
  • A minor / small discrepancy — "There's only a minor discrepancy; it's probably a typo."
  • Discrepancy between X and Y — This is the most common structure. "There's a discrepancy between what he said and what the records show."
Words with Similar Meanings (and How They Differ)

Understanding how "discrepancy" relates to similar words gives you a sharper grasp of it.

  • Inconsistency — Similar, but often refers to something that contradicts itself over time or within a single source. A person can have an inconsistency in their story (it contradicts itself). A discrepancy usually involves two separate things being compared and not matching.
  • Contradiction — Stronger than a discrepancy. A contradiction means two things are completely opposite or mutually exclusive — they can't both be true. A discrepancy just means they don't match up; they could still both be partially true, or one could be a simple error.
  • Gap — More informal and often refers to a difference in quantity or level (a "gap" in knowledge, a "gap" in salary). Less formal than discrepancy and doesn't always carry the sense that something should have matched.
  • Mismatch — Casual and straightforward. A discrepancy often implies a need for investigation or explanation; a mismatch is more neutral and just notes that two things don't fit.
A One-Sentence Summary to Lock It In

A discrepancy is a difference between two things that should agree or match — and because they don't, it signals a problem, an error, or something that needs to be looked into.

If you ever feel unsure about the word, come back to that sentence. It holds everything.
4484:
"Discrete" means separate, individually distinct, and not connected to or blending into anything else.

When things are discrete, each one is its own clearly bounded unit. There are definite gaps or divisions between them. Nothing flows continuously from one to the other.

Think of eggs in a carton. Each egg is its own separate object. You can count them: one, two, three. There is no ambiguity about where one egg ends and another begins. They don't merge into each other. That is what "discrete" captures — things that are cleanly separated into countable, distinct units.

Now contrast that with water poured into a glass. You cannot point to "the first water" and "the second water" — it all blends into one continuous whole. Water in a glass is the opposite of discrete.

The word stresses two things at once:

  1. Separateness — the items do not blend, merge, or flow into one another.
  2. Individuality — each item can be identified, pointed to, or counted as its own thing.

Both ideas are always present. Something is not "discrete" just because it's separate (a person standing alone is separate, but we wouldn't normally call them "discrete"). The word is used when you are drawing attention to the fact that something exists as a series or set of individual, non-overlapping units, as opposed to a continuous whole.

• "The course is divided into five discrete modules."
    Each module is its own self-contained unit. They don't overlap or blend together. You can clearly say "I am in module 3."
  • "The doctor identified three discrete tumors, not one large mass."
    Each tumor is a separate, bounded thing. They are not connected to each other.
  • "Music is made up of discrete notes."
    Each note — C, D, E — is its own distinct sound. Even though notes played in sequence can feel smooth, each one is a separate, definable unit.
  • "The government handles this through several discrete departments."
    Each department is its own separate unit with its own function and boundary.
  • "The spectrum of light is continuous, but we divide it into discrete colors for convenience."
    Here, "discrete" is being contrasted with "continuous." We carve out named colors (red, orange, yellow…), but the underlying spectrum has no real breaks.

You will encounter this word most frequently in:

  • Mathematics and science — "discrete mathematics" deals with things that can be counted (whole numbers, graphs, sets), as opposed to calculus which deals with continuous change. "Discrete data" means data that takes specific, separate values (like the number of students in a class: 28, 29, 30 — never 28.7).
  • Technology and computing — computer data is fundamentally discrete. A pixel is a discrete dot. A binary digit (0 or 1) is a discrete value. Digital signals are discrete; analog signals are continuous.
  • Formal writing and academic language — when a writer wants to be precise about the fact that something is made of separate, non-overlapping parts.
The one confusion you must avoid

"Discrete" is almost always confused with "discreet" (spelled with two e's together at the end). They sound identical when spoken, but they mean completely different things:

  • Discrete (this word) = separate, individually distinct
  • Discreet = careful and tactful, not drawing attention to sensitive things (e.g., "She was discreet about his personal problems.")

They share no overlap in meaning whatsoever. The only connection is that both come from the same Latin root historically — but in modern English, they are two entirely different words that happen to sound the same. When you see "discrete" in a technical, scientific, or academic context, it always means separate and distinct, never anything about being secretive or tactful.

A simple trick to remember which is which: discr*e*t*e* has the letters separated (e…e, with letters in between) — just like its meaning, things that are separated.
The spectrum of use: from casual to technical

At its most casual, you might say:
"She had two discrete problems to solve — the deadline and the budget."
(Meaning: two separate, independent issues, not one tangled mess.)

At its most technical, a mathematician might say:
"The set of natural numbers is a discrete set."
(Meaning: each number is a distinct, isolated point on the number line, with gaps between them.)

The core meaning is exactly the same in both cases. The word just carries more weight and precision in technical fields because the distinction between "discrete" and "continuous" is fundamental to those fields.
Discrete means consisting of separate, individually distinct units that do not blend into or connect with each other — the opposite of something continuous or merged.
4485: Discretion has two closely related meanings, and both revolve around one central idea: good judgment. One meaning is about how you behave (carefully and wisely), and the other is about the power you have (the freedom to make your own call).
Meaning 1: Careful, Tactful, and Private Behavior

This is the more common everyday meaning. When someone shows discretion, it means they are careful and wise about what they say, what they share, and how they act — especially in sensitive or delicate situations.

Think of it this way: some information is private, some situations are fragile, and some moments require you to stay quiet rather than speak up. A person who handles these moments with discretion knows exactly what to say, what not to say, and how to behave so that no harm, embarrassment, or damage is caused.

Key qualities that make up discretion in this sense:

  • Knowing when to keep quiet. If your friend tells you something personal and asks you not to share it, and you don't — that's discretion.
  • Not drawing unnecessary attention. If you notice your colleague made a mistake in a meeting, discretion means you bring it up privately later rather than calling them out in front of everyone.
  • Being trustworthy with sensitive information. A doctor knows private things about patients. A lawyer knows private things about clients. They are expected to handle that information with discretion — meaning they don't gossip, don't share carelessly, and treat it with respect.
  • Reading the room. Discretion also involves knowing when a topic is inappropriate, when a joke is out of place, or when silence is wiser than speech.

Examples:

  • "She showed great discretion by not mentioning the argument in front of the children."
  • "The journalist used discretion and chose not to publish certain details that could harm innocent people."
  • "He handled the scandal with discretion, avoiding unnecessary drama."
  • "We need someone who can be trusted to act with discretion in this role."

The opposite of this kind of discretion is being indiscreet — blurting things out, sharing secrets, saying the wrong thing at the wrong time, or handling sensitive matters carelessly.
Meaning 2: The Freedom or Power to Make Your Own Judgment

The second meaning shifts from behavior to authority and freedom. Here, discretion means the right or power to decide something yourself, based on your own judgment — without being forced to follow a strict rule.

When someone has discretion over something, it means the decision is theirs to make. There is no single fixed answer. They get to weigh the situation and choose what they think is best.

Examples:

  • "The judge has discretion when it comes to sentencing — she can give a lighter or heavier penalty based on the specific case."
  • "Employees are given discretion over how they organize their workday."
  • "The scholarship committee has full discretion in selecting the winner."
  • "Tips are left at the customer's discretion." (Meaning: it's entirely up to the customer to decide.)

This is where the very common phrase "at someone's discretion" comes from. It simply means: it's up to that person to decide.

  • "Dress code is at the manager's discretion." → The manager decides.
  • "Extra credit is awarded at the teacher's discretion." → The teacher decides, case by case.
  • "Entry is at the bouncer's discretion." → The bouncer makes the call.

Another common instruction you'll hear is "use your discretion" — which means: don't wait for someone to spell out every rule; use your own good judgment to figure out what's right in this situation.

At first glance, these two meanings might seem unrelated. But they share a deep common thread: judgment.

  • In Meaning 1, discretion means using good judgment about how to behave — what to say, what to keep quiet, how to handle sensitive things wisely.
  • In Meaning 2, discretion means having the authority to use your own judgment — the power to make a decision without being forced down a fixed path.

In both cases, the word is pointing toward a person who thinks carefully, reads situations well, and acts wisely rather than rashly.

"With discretion"
Means carefully, privately, and tactfully.
"Please handle this matter with discretion."

"At someone's discretion"
Means it is up to that person to decide.
"Refunds are issued at the manager's discretion."

"Use your discretion"
Means make your own wise judgment.
"The guidelines are flexible — just use your discretion."

"Discretion is advised"
A warning that the content ahead may be sensitive, and you should judge whether it's appropriate for you (or those around you).
"Viewer discretion is advised" — a phrase you often see before mature content on television.

"Discretion is the better part of valor"
A well-known proverb meaning that it is sometimes wiser and braver to be cautious and hold back than to act boldly. True courage includes knowing when not to act.

• Discreet (adjective): The describing word. A discreet person is one who has discretion — careful, tactful, and trustworthy. "She was very discreet about what she knew."
  • Indiscretion (noun): The opposite of discretion — a careless, thoughtless act or remark, especially one that reveals something private. "His indiscretion cost him his career."
  • Discretionary (adjective): Describes something that is left to someone's own judgment or choice. "Discretionary spending" means money you choose to spend (as opposed to money you must spend on necessities).
A Quick Way to Remember It

Think of discretion as having two faces, one soul:

Face 1 → "I know what NOT to say or do here." (careful, private behavior)

Face 2 → "It's MY call to make." (freedom of judgment)

Both faces show a person who is thoughtful, trusted, and wise. That's the soul of the word.
4486:
Something is discretionary when it is not fixed, not forced, and not automatic — it depends entirely on the judgment and choice of the person or authority who has the power to decide.

In other words: no rule, law, or obligation requires it to happen in a particular way. The decision is left open, and whoever holds the relevant authority gets to decide whether to act, how much to act, or when to act — based on their own assessment of the situation.

The clearest way to grasp "discretionary" is by placing it next to its opposite.

  • Mandatory (compulsory): Must happen. There is no choice. The outcome is pre-determined by a rule, law, or contract.
  • Discretionary: May or may not happen, or may happen to varying degrees. The outcome depends on someone's judgment.

If your employer is required by law to pay you a certain minimum wage, that payment is mandatory — not discretionary. But if your employer chooses to give you a year-end bonus based on how well the company performed and how they feel about your work, that bonus is discretionary — they decide its size, or even whether to give it at all.
What Makes Something "Discretionary"? Two Things Working Together

When we call something discretionary, two ideas are always present:

  1. Freedom: There is genuine latitude to choose. No external rule locks the outcome in advance.
  2. Judgment: That freedom isn't random or arbitrary. The person exercising it is expected to think carefully and decide wisely. Discretionary power comes with an implied responsibility to use good judgment.

This is an important nuance. Discretionary does not mean "whatever you feel like." It means: you have the freedom to decide, and you're expected to decide thoughtfully.
Where You'll See This Word Used

1. Money and Finance

This is one of the most common areas.

  • Discretionary income / discretionary spending: The money left over after you've paid for all your necessities — rent, food, utilities, loan repayments. Because you are not obligated to spend this money on any particular thing, it is "discretionary." You can save it, travel with it, spend it on entertainment, or do anything you judge best. No bill is waiting for it.
  • Discretionary budget: A portion of a company's or government's budget that is not pre-committed to fixed expenses. It can be allocated at the decision-maker's judgment — to new projects, emergencies, or opportunities that arise.
  • Discretionary bonus: A bonus that an employer is not contractually required to pay. Whether they give it, and how much, is entirely up to their decision. Because it's not guaranteed, you can't count on it the way you count on your fixed salary.
  • Discretionary fund: A reserve of money that a person or organization can use at their own discretion, without needing prior approval or being bound to spend it on specific things.

2. Authority and Power (Law, Government, Management)

  • Discretionary powers / discretionary authority: When a judge, police officer, government official, or manager is given "discretionary powers," it means they are authorized to make decisions on a case-by-case basis using their own judgment. The rules don't dictate a single mandatory outcome; they give the authority figure room to weigh the circumstances and decide.
    For example: A judge may have discretionary authority in sentencing. Two people may commit the same crime, but the judge can look at each person's circumstances — history, intent, remorse — and choose a sentence they find appropriate, within legal limits. The sentence is not mechanically pre-determined.
  • Discretionary decision: Any decision that is made based on the decision-maker's own judgment rather than by following a fixed rule.

3. Everyday and General Use

  • "Attendance at the optional seminar is discretionary." (You decide whether to go — no one is forcing you.)
  • "The doctor may, at her discretionary judgment, prescribe a lower dose." (She has the freedom and responsibility to decide what's right for the patient.)
  • "Tipping at restaurants is generally discretionary." (No law requires it; you decide whether to tip and how much, based on your judgment of the service.)

This matters because learners sometimes misread it:

  • It does not mean "unimportant." Discretionary decisions can be very significant. A judge's discretionary sentencing decision can affect someone's entire life.
  • It does not mean "random" or "arbitrary." A discretionary choice is made by a thinking person using judgment. It's the opposite of random — it's considered.
  • It does not mean "definitely won't happen." It means it might or might not happen, or the amount isn't fixed. The person with the authority decides.
  • It does not mean "optional in a lazy sense." It means the obligation is open-ended and judgment-dependent, not that the matter is trivial.

One useful thing to notice is that discretionary power can be wide or narrow.

  • Wide discretionary power: "The committee may allocate these funds however it sees fit." → Almost unlimited judgment.
  • Narrow discretionary power: "The officer may issue a warning instead of a fine, but only for first-time offenders." → Judgment allowed, but within tight conditions.

In both cases, the word "discretionary" still applies — but the scope of freedom differs. Context usually tells you how wide or narrow that freedom is.

Discretionary = left to someone's own judgment and choice, rather than being fixed, automatic, or mandatory.

When something is discretionary, no pre-set rule determines the outcome. A person or authority with the relevant power gets to look at the situation, weigh it, and decide — whether to act, how much, or in what way. That freedom always comes paired with an expectation of good judgment.
4487:
The adjective discriminate means: carefully selective; making thoughtful distinctions. It describes something (or someone) that is not random, not careless, but precise — showing the ability to tell things apart and choose wisely among them.

Think of it this way: to discriminate between things means to recognize real differences between them. So when you describe something as discriminate, you're saying it reflects that careful, deliberate recognition of differences.
What It Really Means — Going Deeper

The adjective carries two closely related ideas bundled together:

1. Selectivity — not grabbing everything indiscriminately, but choosing with purpose.
2. Discernment — the ability to notice fine distinctions that others might miss.

When a person or action is called discriminate, it signals a kind of intellectual precision — the quality of being able to separate the good from the bad, the relevant from the irrelevant, the worthy from the unworthy.

A discriminate reader doesn't read every book thrown at them — they read thoughtfully, selecting books that deserve their attention.

A discriminate use of language means choosing words carefully, with awareness of their exact meaning — not using them loosely or carelessly.

• "She was a discriminate collector of antiques, buying only pieces with genuine historical value."
    (She didn't buy randomly; she had the judgment to distinguish truly valuable items from imposters.)
  • "The general issued discriminate orders — only specific targets were to be engaged, nothing indiscriminate."
    (The orders were precise and selective, not broad and sweeping.)
  • "His discriminate praise made it all the more meaningful — he didn't compliment everyone."
    (He praised only what truly deserved praise, so when he said something was good, you knew he meant it.)
  • "A discriminate mind approaches problems methodically, separating facts from assumptions."
    (A careful, precise mind — one that draws sharp distinctions.)

This is important to understand. In everyday speech, the verb "to discriminate" often carries a negative meaning — treating someone unfairly because of their race, gender, religion, etc. But the adjective form is positive (or at worst neutral).

Calling someone discriminate is a compliment. It means they have good judgment. They are not easily fooled. They can tell quality from mediocrity, truth from falsehood, the essential from the trivial.

The cleanest way to understand any word is through its opposite, and here the contrast is very sharp.

Indiscriminate = random, without distinction, careless, making no effort to separate one thing from another.
Discriminate = the exact opposite — deliberate, precise, making careful distinctions.

An indiscriminate bombing attacks everything — civilians, military targets, fields, hospitals — without distinction. A discriminate bombing (in theory) targets only specific military objectives, avoiding everything else.

An indiscriminate eater will eat anything put in front of them. A discriminate eater notices flavor, texture, quality — and chooses accordingly.

You will often encounter the closely related adjective discriminating, which carries almost the same meaning and is arguably more commonly used in modern English.

  • A discriminating reader = a discriminate reader
  • A discriminating palate = an ability to detect fine differences in taste

Both words point to the same quality. "Discriminating" emphasizes the active exercise of that judgment; "discriminate" emphasizes that the choice or action itself reflects such judgment. In practice, the two are nearly interchangeable in most contexts.

What it meansCareful, thoughtful, selective; showing the ability to tell things apart and make precise distinctions
TonePositive — a mark of intelligence, taste, and good judgment
Who or what can be "discriminate"?A person's taste, judgment, choices, praise, reading habits, use of language, actions, etc.
Key quality it signalsPrecision over randomness; thought over carelessness

The adjective discriminate essentially honors the human capacity to see clearly — to not lump everything together, to resist the lazy impulse to treat all things as equal, and instead to recognize real differences with care and intelligence.
4488:
Discriminate means to notice a difference and act on it — either by telling things apart, or by treating people differently based on some characteristic.

That one core idea — noticing a difference and acting on it — splits into two very distinct uses, and it's crucial to understand both.

In this sense, discriminate simply means to recognize or identify the difference between two or more things. There is nothing negative about it here.

Pattern: discriminate between things

Examples:

  • A professional wine taster can discriminate between a cheap wine and an expensive one just by smell.
  • A good doctor can discriminate between a viral infection and a bacterial one.
  • Young children often cannot discriminate between fantasy and reality.

Here, discriminating is actually a skill. It means you are sharp enough to notice differences that others might miss. Think of it as the mental act of sorting — your brain is carefully separating one thing from another based on real, observable differences.

This is the more commonly heard use today, and it carries a strongly negative meaning. Here, discriminate means to treat a person or group of people unfairly or unequally based on a characteristic they belong to — such as their race, gender, religion, age, disability, nationality, or sexual orientation.

Pattern: discriminate against someone

Examples:

  • The company was sued for discriminating against women during the hiring process.
  • It is illegal in many countries to discriminate against people because of their religion.
  • He felt he was being discriminated against at work because of his age.

Notice the key phrase: "discriminate against." This tells you straight away that you are in the negative sense of the word. Someone is being treated worse — denied a job, excluded from a place, denied rights, or treated with hostility — not because of anything they did, but simply because of who they are or what group they belong to.

The critical thing here is that the difference being acted upon is unjust and irrelevant. A company might say "we don't hire people over 50" — the person's age has nothing fair to do with their ability to do the job. That is discrimination.
The Key Difference Between the Two Senses

Both senses involve noticing a difference and acting on it, but here is what separates them:

Sense 1 (neutral): The differences you notice are real and relevant, and you are simply exercising judgment or perception. A chef discriminates between fresh and stale ingredients — the difference genuinely matters.

Sense 2 (negative): The characteristic you act on is irrelevant to the situation, and someone is treated worse because of it. An employer discriminating against a candidate because of their skin color — the skin color has nothing to do with the job.

In short: one is a skill, the other is an injustice.

When the word is used as an adjective — a discriminating person — it almost always means someone who has refined taste and sharp judgment. It comes from Sense 1.

  • She is a discriminating reader — she knows good writing from bad.
  • He has a discriminating eye for art — he can spot quality and flaw alike.

This is a compliment. A discriminating person is someone who doesn't accept everything at face value; they can tell the excellent from the mediocre.

Since you'll encounter this closely, it's worth noting: the noun form is discrimination, and it follows the same two senses.

  • "Color discrimination" — the ability of the eye to tell colors apart (Sense 1, neutral).
  • "Racial discrimination" — treating people unequally based on race (Sense 2, negative).

In everyday conversation, when people say "discrimination" without any qualifier, they almost always mean the negative sense — unfair treatment of people.
Common Collocations (Words That Go With It)

These are the most natural word pairings you'll see:

  • discriminate between → used in the neutral sense (discriminate between right and wrong)
  • discriminate against → used in the negative sense (discriminate against minorities)
  • racial / gender / age / religious discrimination → specifies what the unfair treatment is based on
  • a discriminating taste / eye / palate → high standards and sharp judgment (always positive)

Discriminate between thingsNeutral — to notice and tell apart real differences. A skill.
Discriminate against peopleNegative — to treat unfairly based on irrelevant characteristics. An injustice.
Discriminating (adjective)Positive — having sharp judgment and refined taste.
One Sentence to Remember It All
Discriminate means to act on a noticed difference — wisely, when you use it to tell things apart; unjustly, when you use it to treat a person worse because of who they are.
4489:
When we call someone discriminating, we mean they have the sharp ability to notice fine differences between things — and because of that, they have excellent, refined taste and judgment. They don't just accept anything that comes their way. They carefully evaluate, compare, and choose only what is truly good or of high quality.

Think of it this way: imagine two people walking into an art gallery.

  • Person A glances around and says, "Yeah, these all look like nice paintings to me."
  • Person B studies each painting and says, "This one has exceptional brushwork, this one has a poorly balanced composition, and this one — this one is a masterpiece."

Person B is the discriminating one. They can see differences that others miss, and their judgment is sharper for it.

The word rests on two ideas working together:

1. The ability to tell things apart
A discriminating person can detect subtle differences — in quality, style, value, flavor, craftsmanship — that an ordinary or careless observer would completely overlook.

2. Refined selectivity as a result
Because they can tell things apart so well, they are very selective. They have high standards. They won't settle for something mediocre when they know what excellent looks like.

Together, these make "discriminating" a word that describes someone with a sophisticated, well-trained sense of quality and judgment.

"Discriminating" almost always appears before a noun, describing a person's faculty of judgment in a particular area. The most common combinations you'll encounter are:

  • A discriminating taste — someone who can tell the difference between good food, wine, music, or art and something merely average.
  • A discriminating eye — someone who can visually spot quality, flaws, or excellence with precision.
  • A discriminating palate — specifically used for food and drink; someone who can detect subtle flavors others can't.
  • A discriminating reader — someone who critically evaluates what they read rather than accepting everything at face value.
  • A discriminating buyer/collector — someone who carefully selects only the finest items and won't be fooled by inferior goods.

• "The restaurant was designed to please even the most discriminating food lovers."

(It was so good, it could satisfy even people with very high, refined standards.)

  • "She was a discriminating collector who only purchased paintings she considered true masterpieces."

(She was so skilled at judging quality that she was very selective in what she bought.)

  • "The editor had a discriminating eye — he could spot a weak paragraph instantly, no matter how polished it appeared."

(His judgment was sharp enough to catch flaws others would miss.)

  • "Wine critics must have a discriminating palate to do their job well."

(They need the refined ability to detect subtle differences in flavor.)

This is important — "discriminating" in its adjective form is a positive, respectful word. Calling someone discriminating is a compliment. You are saying they have developed, refined judgment. You are saying they are not fooled easily. You are saying they know quality when they see it.

If someone says you have a "discriminating taste," they are praising you — suggesting that your sense of quality is so well-developed that you can spot what's genuinely good and reject what isn't.
What It Does NOT Mean (A Critical Distinction)

Here is where many learners get confused. You may know that "discrimination" can be a very negative word — as in treating people unfairly because of their race, gender, religion, etc. That is a completely different sense of the word.

When "discriminating" is used as an adjective to describe a person's taste, eye, palate, or judgment, it carries no negative meaning at all. It simply means having the refined ability to tell apart quality from mediocrity.

The negative social meaning belongs to the word "discriminatory" (e.g., "discriminatory policies"), not to "discriminating" in this adjective form.

Knowing these will help you see the word from different angles:

  • Discerning — the closest synonym; almost interchangeable
  • Selective — emphasizes being choosy and not accepting just anything
  • Perceptive — able to notice things others miss
  • Refined — having cultured, polished taste
  • Particular — very careful and exact about choices
  • Fastidious — extremely attentive to quality and detail (slightly stronger)
  • Judicious — showing sound judgment

• Undiscriminating — accepting anything without careful judgment
  • Indiscriminate — making choices randomly or carelessly, without considering quality or distinctions
  • Unselective — not choosy; accepting whatever comes
A Simple Mental Image to Lock It In

Picture a jeweler examining diamonds. While most people just see a shiny stone, the jeweler holds it under a loupe and can immediately spot the cut quality, the clarity, the tiny flaws, and the brilliance that separates a gem worth $500 from one worth $50,000.

That jeweler is discriminating. Their trained perception allows them to see what others cannot — and that refined judgment makes them highly selective in what they approve of.

Whenever you see the word "discriminating" used as an adjective, picture that jeweler: someone whose judgment is sharp enough to see what others miss, and selective enough to choose only the finest.
